clinicalPearls: ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion, defined by isolated thrombocytopenia with an otherwise normal full blood count and blood film and no alternative explanation.
It is mediated by antiplatelet autoantibodies that cause accelerated splenic destruction of platelets and also impair megakaryocyte platelet production.

It may be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and lymphoma, HIV, hepatitis C, Helicobacter pylori, drugs or common variable immunodeficiency.
Bleeding is typically mucocutaneous, with petechiae, purpura, epistaxis and menorrhagia, and the risk of serious internal bleeding correlates only loosely with the platelet count.
Childhood ITP is usually acute and self-limiting, often following a viral illness, whereas adult ITP more often runs a chronic course.
Bone marrow examination is not required in typical cases but is considered where features are atypical, before splenectomy, or in older patients to exclude myelodysplasia.
Treatment (corticosteroids with or without intravenous immunoglobulin) is reserved for significant bleeding or a very low count, and many patients can safely be observed.
Second-line options include thrombopoietin receptor agonists, rituximab and splenectomy, and the therapeutic aim is a safe haemostatic count rather than a normal platelet count.
reference.pathophysiology: ITP arises from a loss of immune tolerance to platelet surface antigens, generating IgG autoantibodies directed chiefly against the platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa and Ib/IX complexes. Antibody-coated platelets are recognised by Fc receptors on splenic and hepatic macrophages and cleared prematurely, shortening platelet lifespan. The same autoantibodies and dysregulated T-cell responses also act on megakaryocytes to impair platelet production, so the marrow response is inappropriately blunted rather than compensatory. Cytotoxic T lymphocytes and abnormalities of regulatory T-cell function contribute to the sustained autoimmune process, and in secondary ITP an underlying infection, lymphoproliferative disorder, autoimmune disease or drug drives the antiplatelet response.
additionalDifferentials: pseudothrombocytopenia due to EDTA-induced platelet clumping
myelodysplasia or other marrow failure and infiltration
thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura or haemolytic uraemic syndrome
additionalInvestigations: full blood count and blood film to confirm true isolated thrombocytopenia and exclude clumping or blasts
direct antiglobulin test where there is coexisting anaemia (to detect Evans syndrome)
bone marrow examination in atypical presentations or older patients
redFlags: headache, vomiting or focal neurology suggesting intracranial haemorrhage
gastrointestinal bleeding such as melaena or haematemesis
extensive wet purpura with mucosal (buccal or gingival) bleeding
profound thrombocytopenia accompanied by active bleeding
reference.prognosis: The overall outlook is good; most children remit spontaneously within weeks to months, and although adult disease is frequently chronic it is usually manageable, with serious haemorrhage being uncommon.
pitfalls: missing pseudothrombocytopenia and treating a spurious low count caused by EDTA-dependent clumping
over-treating asymptomatic mild thrombocytopenia rather than observing
failing to look for secondary causes such as HIV, hepatitis C, lupus or a lymphoproliferative disorder
expecting platelet transfusion to be effective outside life-threatening bleeding, when transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed
overlooking myelodysplasia in an older patient with apparently isolated thrombocytopenia

management: Observation alone for patients with mild thrombocytopenia and no significant bleeding, as many require no treatment
Corticosteroids (prednisolone or dexamethasone) as first-line therapy, with intravenous immunoglobulin when a rapid platelet rise is needed
Second-line options including thrombopoietin receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim), rituximab or splenectomy for chronic or refractory disease
For life-threatening haemorrhage, combined platelet transfusion, intravenous immunoglobulin and intravenous corticosteroids, with tranexamic acid as an adjunct
Identify and treat secondary causes, including Helicobacter pylori eradication and antiviral therapy for HIV or hepatitis C
Advise avoidance of antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs and take contact-injury precautions while thrombocytopenic
Monitor the full blood count to guide treatment and detect relapse, involving haematology for diagnostic uncertainty or refractory disease
